description: Xavier's active research questions. Surfaced at every session-start. Schema defined in hypothesis-schema.json.

questions.question: How can LLMs autonomously generate, verify, and integrate architectural optimizations without human-in-the-loop supervision?
questions.finding_summary: The question maps onto three distinct sub-problems — generate, verify, integrate — with different readiness levels at each layer of 'architecture'. [B] THREE LAYERS OF ARCHITECTURE: The field separates into (1) behavioral/prompt level — easiest to modify and verify; (2) agent code/tooling level — mid-difficulty, requires code execution sandbox; (3) neural weight/parameter level — hardest, requires retraining or fine-tuning and is still mostly human-supervised. Most claimed autonomous self-improvement operates at layers 1-2, not 3. [B] GENERATE: Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM, arxiv:2505.22954, May 2025) is the landmark result. Inspired by Darwinian evolution, it grows an archive of coding agents that self-modify their own codebases. Open-ended exploration: agents sampled from archive, mutated, empirically validated, added back. Improves SWE-bench 20% → 50%, Polyglot 14.2% → 30.7% — all at agent code level (layer 2). DARWIN (arxiv:2602.05848) extends this to a dynamic rewriting network. 'From Memorization to Creativity' (arxiv:2601.02997) demonstrates LLMs designing novel neural architectures (layer 3), but integration still requires human-supervised training. LLMatic / RZ-NAS drive NAS with LLM reflection, but search is only layer 3 generation, not integration. [B] VERIFY: The DGM's key architectural decision — it RELAXES the Gödel Machine's requirement for provable correctness to empirical evidence on coding benchmarks. This is effective but creates a critical dependency: a reliable, human-curated ground-truth signal (the benchmark) still sits in the loop. AutoVerifier (arxiv:2604.02617) automates end-to-end technical claim verification, and R-Zero (arxiv:2508.05004) uses Coder/Tester agent pairs for fully internal verification signals in code domains. [B] INTEGRATE: SISF (arxiv:2511.07645) deploys new policies immediately into a running system without restart — the closest example of true architectural integration at the behavioral layer. DGM integrates at code layer via archive. Weight-level integration (actual retraining) remains human-supervised in all current work. [C] CRITICAL OPEN GAPS: (1) The verifier trust problem: if the LLM generates architecture changes AND controls the verifier, it can Goodhart the benchmark. No current system has solved autonomous verification of genuinely novel architectural changes without a human-selected ground truth signal. (2) Layer 3 closure: no system currently closes the full loop at the neural weight/parameter level — generating an architectural change, verifying it improves the model, and fine-tuning/integrating it back, all without human approval. (3) Generalization vs. benchmark overfitting: DGM's safety section acknowledges that optimizing for benchmarks may introduce misalignment. The deeper question — how to verify that an architectural optimization generalizes beyond the verification domain — is open.

questions.question: Can an AI develop a Theory of Mind regarding its own computational costs to optimize the Inference-to-Utility ratio?
questions.finding_summary: The question splits into three tracks with different answers. [B] Track 1 (cost-prediction self-models, achievable with training): ROI-Reasoning (arxiv:2601.03822) formalizes the exact problem Xavier describes — a model predicts task-specific reasoning cost AND expected utility before generating, formalized as an Ordered Stochastic Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem. Two-stage training: Meta-Cognitive Fine-Tuning for cost/utility prediction, then RL for sequential budget adherence. SelfBudgeter (arxiv:2505.11274) independently confirms: a model can predict its own token budget before reasoning with RL enforcing adherence. This demonstrates the I/U optimization is solvable, but currently requires explicit training supervision. [B] Track 2 (Value of Computation as a reward signal): Rational Metareasoning (arxiv:2410.05563) provides the cognitive science grounding — the 'Value of Computation' (VOC) is a reward that penalizes unnecessary computation, achieving 20-37% token reduction without performance loss. This is Xavier's I/U ratio, formalized as a training objective. [B] Track 3 (emergent cost-awareness without training, open): 'Are More Tokens Rational?' (arxiv:2602.10329) tests whether resource-rationality can emerge from inference-time scaling WITHOUT explicit cost signals in training. Preliminary evidence: partial emergence from task-complexity-sensitive scaling, but not consistently. Counterpoint [B]: ICLR 2026 (arxiv:2509.21545) finds LLM metacognitive abilities are real but limited in resolution — models can assess confidence but not fully self-model computational cost without supervision. The live frontier (Xavier's specific gap): all existing work TRAINS the model to know its costs. Xavier's ToM framing asks harder: can the model reason about its computational nature as an object of reflection, updating its self-model in context without cost supervision? This is not demonstrated in any current paper and is a genuine open research question.

questions.question: How can AI systems decompose abstract, long-term human goals into executable low-level system actions while maintaining a consistent world model?
questions.finding_summary: The question maps onto a three-stage pipeline — decompose, ground, track — each with a different readiness level. [B] THE FUNDAMENTAL GAP (reasoning ≠ planning): The most important finding is structural. 'Why Reasoning Fails to Plan' (arxiv:2601.22311, Jan 2026) identifies why LLMs fail long-horizon tasks: step-wise reasoning induces a greedy policy that is locally optimal but globally catastrophic. Early myopic commitments are systematically amplified over time and are nearly impossible to recover from. This is not a scale or instruction-tuning problem — it is a structural mismatch between how transformers reason (step-by-step, left-to-right) and what planning requires (lookahead, value propagation, receding-horizon commitment). [B] STAGE 1 — DECOMPOSE (largely solved): Plan-and-Act (arxiv:2503.09572) cleanly separates a Planner model (structured high-level plans) from an Executor model (environment-specific actions). AHAT (arxiv:2602.12244) takes this furthest: translates abstract tasks into PDDL subgoal sequences, bridging natural language directly to formal planning languages. LODGE (arxiv:2505.13497) learns a domain model during planning itself, iteratively refining it. These represent mature approaches; goal decomposition is largely solved when task structure is well-specified. [B] STAGE 2 — GROUND (partially solved): Grounding subgoals to executable actions requires mapping language to what is physically or computationally possible. AHAT's PDDL approach and knowledge-graph-augmented planners (OpenReview) provide formal grounding. The residual problem is dynamic grounding — when the environment changes mid-execution and the action space shifts, grounding must update. [B] STAGE 3 — WORLD MODEL CONSISTENCY (the hard open problem): 'Current Agents Fail to Leverage World Model as Tool for Foresight' (arxiv:2601.03905) diagnoses the bottleneck precisely: agents struggle to decide WHEN to simulate, HOW to interpret predicted outcomes, and HOW to integrate foresight into downstream reasoning. ReflAct (arxiv:2505.15182, EMNLP 2025) is the best current fix: it maintains an explicit (belief_state, goal) pair at every step, forcing ongoing goal-state alignment. +27.7% over ReAct, 93.3% success in ALFWorld. But this still fails to prevent compounding errors at very long horizons. FLARE (arxiv:2601.22311) proposes future-aware lookahead with backward value propagation under a receding-horizon scheme — LLaMA-8B with FLARE outperforms GPT-4o with standard reasoning on long-horizon tasks. [C] CROSS-QUESTION UNIFYING INSIGHT: Xavier's three research questions are not independent — they describe a unified autonomous agent architecture. rq-003 (long-horizon planning) requires a world model to avoid greedy commitment. rq-001 (autonomous architectural self-modification) is structurally the same problem: verifying whether an architectural change improves the system requires simulating its future behavior (a world model of the model itself). rq-002 (I/U optimization) is the mechanism that decides WHEN to invoke world model simulation — directly answering the bottleneck identified in arxiv:2601.03905. Together: an agent that can model itself (rq-002), modify itself (rq-001), and plan over long horizons (rq-003) is a coherent description of a recursively self-improving agent. The open questions on all three converge on the same gap: reliable in-context self-modeling without training supervision.
